study: Elder, Scarcity and Prosperity in Postwar Childbearing
exposure_measure: Depression deprivation of the parental household vs postwar prosperity
design: two-cohort life-course comparison (Oakland b.1920-21, Berkeley b.1928-29)
estimator_class: adjusted means with class origin as covariate
magnitude: completed family size mean 2.9 both cohorts; adult status x deprivation interaction p<.10; intergenerational correlation of family size <.12
notes: Descriptive/ANOVA, not an Easterlin test as such. The benchmark (Depression scarcity in the household of origin) is measured rather than proxied, which is why it is in this cell. No effect estimate on a relative-income parameter.

study: Behrman & Taubman, A Test of the Easterlin Fertility Model Using Income for Two Generations
period: offspring b. ~1953, completed fertility observed to 1980s
exposure_measure: income of parents AND grandparents (two generations observed directly)
design: NAS-NRC twin registry + offspring survey, N=1463 couples
estimator_class: OLS with Heckman selection correction (probit for subsample inclusion)
magnitude: parents' income -0.032 (t=1.5); grandparents' income -1.0 (t=0.7) and 0.92 (t=0.7); own income NOT positively significant; R2=0.04
notes: THE decisive record for this cell. The only study with income for two generations, i.e. the only direct test of Easterlin's own benchmark. Authors' verdict: the test 'favors the Becker formulation'. Selection is acknowledged and corrected; the twin sample is censored (both twins healthy enough for military service).

study: Comolli, Resources, aspirations and first births during the Great Recession
exposure_measure: own occupational prestige relative to the parental household's when growing up (intergenerational mobility)
design: event history on PSID 2003-2017; men N=2709 subjects/184672 person-months, women N=2956/218348
magnitude: relative status HR 1.17*** (1.05-1.31) to 1.27*** (1.11-1.45) for men across specifications; attenuates and loses significance in younger-cohort and working-only subsamples (1.12, 1.21, 1.26, all ns)
notes: Supports the mechanism: holding a position as prestigious as one's parents' raises first-birth hazard vs downward mobility. Moderated by aggregate labour-market conditions, differently for men and women.

study: Macunovich, The Missing Factor: Variations in the Income Effect of the Female Wage on Fertility
exposure_measure: income of young males relative to their families' income (logRY), interacted with the female wage
design: aggregate annual time-series regression with a relative-income x female-wage interaction
magnitude: relative income logRY +0.175** (SE 0.082); interaction logRY*logW -20.18*** (2.01); female wage logW -14.59*** (1.15); R2 0.95-0.955. Author's claim: relative income plus the female wage explain 97-99% of variation in fertility, female enrolment and FLFP
notes: The horse race run the other way: argues the female wage's effect on fertility is CONDITIONAL on male relative income, and reports the implied female-wage coefficient moving from -3.31 (1969) to -0.58 (1980) as relative income changes. Read from an OCR'd working paper; coefficients need RA verification.

study: Diebolt & Doliger, Becker vs. Easterlin: Education, Fertility and Growth in France after WWII
exposure_measure: education, fertility, infant mortality, FLFP in a causality/variance-decomposition system
design: time-series causality tests and variance decomposition
magnitude: no single effect estimate; reports a variance decomposition of education
notes: Explicitly a Becker-vs-Easterlin horse race and it declines to pick a winner: the authors conclude the two schools are 'similar and complementary'. A null result for the horse race, which is itself informative for Wall 5.

study: Suzuki, Structural Changes in the Patterns of Japanese Fertility
exposure_measure: husband's income and wife's wages (Butz-Ward), plus female marriage rate
design: prefecture-level panel, 47 prefectures x subperiods, N=506
estimator_class: panel regression with time effects; Chow test for structural break
magnitude: Chow test F=64.61 (p<0.001) for a structural break between 1975 and 1980; female marriage rate 2.025*** (0.328); female wage x marriage rate -0.146 (0.169) ns; authors note one coefficient's 'sign is the opposite of what we expected'
notes: Applies Butz-Ward rather than Easterlin, so it is a rival-model application rather than a head-to-head. The measured STRUCTURAL BREAK at 1975-80 is independently interesting: it is the same hinge at which the scope's own sign test says the Easterlin mechanism stops working.

study: Coskun & Dalgic, The Emergence of Procyclical Fertility
exposure_measure: gender differences in employment risk over the cycle (women's breadwinner status)
design: US state panel with industry employment-cycle correlations
estimator_class: panel regression with controls for income level and female participation
magnitude: significant negative coefficient: more procyclical fertility in states with a more countercyclical gender employment gap
notes: Argues fertility has become PROcyclical, i.e. the opposite of Butz-Ward's countercyclical claim AND not what Easterlin's cohort mechanism predicts either. Directly relevant to the post-1980 window where the scope's sign test fails.

study: Pampel, Relative Cohort Size and Fertility: The Socio-Political Context of the Easterlin Effect
exposure_measure: relative cohort size lagged 2 years, DEFINED AS persons 30-64 over younger adults (the INVERSE of the young/prime ratio)
design: cross-national pooled time-series, 18 countries x 1951-86, with country-specific effects
estimator_class: fixed-effect OLS and fixed-effect GLS; Granger causality analysis reported separately
magnitude: relative cohort size(t-2): +1.87*** (FE OLS), +0.629*** (FE GLS). Country-specific effects range from Canada +3.10*** and Australia +0.891** to Denmark -0.813** and Belgium -0.145 (ns in OLS). Interactions: x social security spending +0.019** (3.23), +0.018* (2.31), +0.010* (2.15); x GDP -0.064*** (5.08) in one specification, ns in others; x FLFP significant in 3 of 4
notes: THE INSTITUTIONAL-MODERATION RECORD, and scope section 5's overturn-condition (ii). SIGN TRAP: Pampel's relative cohort size is prime-age-over-young, the INVERSE of the young-over-prime ratio used in this chapter's own sign test (script 306). A POSITIVE coefficient here is therefore CONSISTENT with Easterlin's negative prediction. Pooling this coefficient with a young/prime-defined one without re-orienting would flip the sign of the pooled estimate. Flagged for the pooling rule. The moderation result is real: the effect is significantly larger where social security spending is higher, and the country-specific effects are heterogeneous enough to include significant NEGATIVE coefficients.

study: Jeon & Shields, The Easterlin hypothesis in the recent experience of higher-income OECD countries
estimator_class: panel data with linear and squared PPP GDP terms, urbanisation, infant mortality, FLFP controls
magnitude: PPP GDP linear -0.023 (t -2.94) and -0.033 (-5.16) in two specifications, ns in the other two; squared term +0.001 (4.88, 6.62, 3.18, 3.08); urban +0.006. Descriptive: TFR falls 2.04 (1975) to 1.62 (1999) while the age-structure variable falls 0.607 to 0.421 across the same window
notes: DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE SIGN TEST. Their own summary statistics show the exposure and the outcome BOTH falling over 1975-1999 across 23 OECD countries - the same co-movement script 306 measured independently, and the wrong direction for the hypothesis. Authors note the predicted post-bust fertility recovery 'is much smaller than earlier studies predicted' and that validity outside the US 'has been limited'.

study: Jeon & Shields, The Impact of Relative Cohort Size on U.S. Fertility 1913-2001
exposure_measure: relative cohort size and changes in relative cohort size
design: annual US time series 1913-2001, extending Whittington-Alm-Peters (1913-1984)
estimator_class: Johansen cointegration tests plus error-correction model
magnitude: Johansen trace statistics reported against critical values (e.g. at most 2: 87.813 vs 95.754, p=0.155 - not rejecting); ECM terms include d(U t-1) -15.940 (t -2.71). Full ECM 'available upon request' - the paper does not print it
cycle_tested: partly (cointegration/ECM dynamics, not an oscillation test)
notes: Adds the child tax deduction and a 'catching up' alternative. NOTE: the authors state the full ECM estimation is available on request rather than printed, so the central estimates are not fully extractable from the paper as published.

study: Macunovich, Re-Visiting the Easterlin Hypothesis: U.S. Fertility 1968-2010
exposure_measure: relative income (young family income against older family income by schooling group)
benchmark_measured: no (older-cohort family income by schooling is a group-level proxy, not the respondent's own parental household)
outcome_measure: proportion of women with an own child under one year of age
design: CPS microdata, women 0-15 years out of school, N=45,955
estimator_class: robust regression with schooling dummies and years-out-of-school splits
magnitude: schooling-group coefficients 0.027 (t 4.1), 0.084 (13.7), -0.047 (-8.3), -0.117 (-19.8), -0.037 (-6.x) across education categories; Adj R-square 0.074-0.075. Older family income by schooling: <12 yrs 42.2 (SD 14.7) rising to >12 yrs 82.2 (29.4)
notes: The most recent US test by the hypothesis's leading proponent, and it extends through 2010 - i.e. INTO the window where the scope's sign test says the mechanism fails. Adjusted R-squared of 0.074 on microdata is low; the relevant question for demsig route C is how much of the fertility series this explains, not whether coefficients are significant on 46k observations.
